     Long-term U.S. asset returns ROGER G. IBBOTSON, “EXPONENTIAL WEALTH: CENTURIES OF STOCK AND BOND RETURNS” (2026), P. 21   This updated version comes from ”Exponential Wealth,” an authoritative book just published by the CFA Institute, the financial analysts’ group. For decades, stockbrokers and financial planners have used this chart to persuade investors to invest more in stocks.

   And that’s worked out well!

   Will it always?

   Although I’ve consistently argued that long-term investors should keep most of their money in stocks, you can’t just look at the past and pretend that it precisely foretells the future.

   Extra return can only be compensation for taking more risk. In the past, investing in stocks carried a lot of risks that have dwindled or disappeared:

   • Trading was exorbitantly expensive. For an individual buying (or selling) shares in small lots, brokerage costs regularly hit 2% or even more . Even for institutions, brokerage costs could exceed 1%.

   • Funds cost a fortune. For most investors, mutual funds were the only practical way to own a diversified portfolio—but sales loads, or commissions, typically ranged between 5% and 8% up front , plus an annual management fee of 0.5% to 2%.

   • The playing field was tilted. Until the Securities and Exchange Commission imposed Regulation FD in 2000 , companies could disclose material information to certain people without revealing it to everyone at the same time.

   • Taxes took a huge toll. Investment researcher Andrew Ang recently estimated that federal taxes would have chopped down the 10%-plus long-term annualized return on stocks in the chart to 7%. To be sure, tax rates are much lower now than in past decades—but Ang’s numbers exclude state and local income taxes, and future tax rates might well rise again.

   • Spreads were a component of return. Until 1997, stocks traded in price increments of 1/8th, or a “spread” of 12.5 cents. Picture a small-cap stock that closed at its bid price of $1. If a buyer came along the next day and paid the ask price of $1.125, then bang! Just like that, a 12.5% return! Today, when stocks trade in increments of one penny or less , such “bid-ask bounces” are immaterial.

   • Grandma and Grandpa didn’t reinvest their dividends. People who owned individual stocks often had to pay a commission to plow their dividends back into more shares ( even if they owned mutual funds! ). History strongly suggests that most investors took their dividends as cash—which would drastically reshape the chart above. In the real world , that Himalayan upward slope would have looked more like the rolling hills of Ohio.

   Modern markets have mitigated these risks, but there’s an unintended consequence to that. Safer markets that are cheaper to invest in are likely to offer lower future returns, precisely because the risks of the past have faded. We all should celebrate, as I wrote a few years ago, that there’s never been a better time to be an investor . But we should also recognize that the future may be less lucrative.

   This is an edition of the Intelligent Investor newsletter, where Jason Zweig writes twice monthly about investment strategy and how to think about money. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here .

Uncle Sam Says Your Wallet Can Fix It ,” looked at new rule proposals from the SEC that would make it easier for private funds to market to the investing public. The managers of funds offering private equity, private credit, nontraded real estate and other alternative assets say it isn’t fair that pension funds and university endowments have access to such funds while small investors don’t. Do you think it’s unfair? Share your thoughts in the comments or, if you’re reading this as an email, just hit reply.

In Greek, psyche means both ”soul” and ”butterfly.” It is the root of our word psychology. Bond issuers that flit around, instead of being bound by their commitments, are playing a psychologically dangerous game. BROOKLYN MUSEUM   Bonds have been dominating the news lately, with U.S. Treasury yields touching their highest levels in almost a quarter-century and worries that France might even repudiate some of its debt .

   Where does the word bond come from, and what can we learn from its history?

   Probably of Teutonic origin, the word first appeared in Middle English in the early 13th century. Originating around the same time as band , it similarly referred to a restriction on a person’s liberty, like shackles, chains or fetters—a meaning that survives today in variants like bondage. 

   Around 1200, “The Ormulum,” an early religious text, wrote that “Herode band himm with irrene band.” A hymn from around 1250 describes “bondes ben leid on Symeon.”

   Those physical restraints soon assumed another meaning: obligation. Around 1330, Robert Manning of Brunne’s “Story of England” referred to “ye bondes of homage.”

   From there it was a short leap for the word to represent a pledge or a person’s word of honor. The modern phrase “my word is my bond” echoes a version of the Lancelot legend around 1500: “O kingis word shuld be a kingis bonde.”

   By the late 16th century, the word had taken on a specific financial meaning. In Shakespeare’s “The Merchant of Venice,” Shylock agrees to lend Antonio 3,000 ducats for three months if Antonio will “go with me to a notary [and] seal me there your single bond.”

   Shylock’s repayment, if Antonio defaulted, would be “an equal pound of your fair flesh.” Shakespeare probably chose that image deliberately. The word covenant, from the Latin convenire, “to come together,” had been used in English for nearly 300 years, often interchangeably with bond. In the book of Genesis, God sealed the covenant with Abraham by enjoining him to “circumscribe the flesh of your foreskin.” Shylock’s pound of flesh invokes this divine commandment, which would have been familiar to everyone in early modern Europe as governments began using bonds as financial instruments.

   The word bond should remind everyone—borrowers and investors alike—that debt is meant to be a binding commitment. When the issuers of bonds no longer fear having to surrender a pound of flesh and they view their commitment as anything less than binding, bonds become little more than oral promises. And oral promises aren’t worth the paper they aren’t written on.

   This is the latest in a series on the origin and history of financial words. You can read the earlier installments here: 
* hedge fund 
* fund 
* credit 
* volatile 
* realize 
* mania 
* money 
* stock 
* cash 
* inflation 

     Oscar Edward Cesare, “Bonds—Which?” (New York Evening Post, May 18, 1917). The choice here is between buying Liberty Bonds, which financed the U.S. military during World War I, and being shackled by “Prussia,” or Germany. Uncle Sam used to take the bondage thing a lot more seriously. LIBRARY OF CONGRESS       Money Mailbag   Have a question you’d like me to answer?

   Want to weigh in on what you just read? Got a tip on something that I or my colleagues should investigate? Itching to tell me I’m wrong about something?

   Just email intelligentinvestor@wsj.com . Don’t forget to include your name and location.

   Q: Can you help me understand the difference between the 30-day SEC yield and the trailing 12-month distribution yield? Which is more important? 
 —Eric MacGillis, Ohio 

   A: “Yield statistics are often treated as if they’re interchangeable, but they’re really measuring different things,” says Joyce Huang, head of multi-sector fixed-income client portfolio management at Vanguard.

   “For bond funds,” she says, “the 30-day SEC yield is generally the best comparison tool between funds, because it’s standardized.” The SEC yield is based on a Securities and Exchange Commission formula, which you can view in detail on p. 57 of this PDF from the SEC . The SEC yield quantifies the latest 30 days of a portfolio’s investment income net of expenses, annualized. For money-market funds, the equivalent measure is the 7-day SEC yield.

   By contrast, says Huang, “Distribution yield is backward-looking. It annualizes the income actually paid out recently, typically using the last month’s distribution. This measure can be useful because it reflects actual cash investors have recently received, but it may not represent what the funds will earn going forward.”

   That’s especially true, adds Huang, “in a rapidly changing rate environment such as right now,” when “distribution yield can lag the portfolio’s current earning power” as rates rise.

   Here’s another important distinction. For many ETFs , distribution yield includes return of capital and income from trading options contracts, which can vary enormously from month to month—and can also eat away at your principal . Many such funds with high distribution yields in the short run end up producing low or negative total returns in the long run.

   That’s why, as the late financial analyst Raymond DeVoe warned, “More money has been lost reaching for yield than at the point of a gun.”

   Be well and invest well,

   Jason

   — Warren Buffett

Wall Street Words: “Bond”

In Greek, psyche means both ”soul” and ”butterfly.” It is the root of our word psychology. Bond issuers that flit around, instead of being bound by their commitments, are playing a psychologically dangerous game. BROOKLYN MUSEUM
 

Bonds have been dominating the news lately, with U.S. Treasury yields touching their highest levels in almost a quarter-century and worries that France might even repudiate some of its debt.

 

Where does the word bond come from, and what can we learn from its history?

 

Probably of Teutonic origin, the word first appeared in Middle English in the early 13th century. Originating around the same time as band, it similarly referred to a restriction on a person’s liberty, like shackles, chains or fetters—a meaning that survives today in variants like bondage.

 

Around 1200, “The Ormulum,” an early religious text, wrote that “Herode band himm with irrene band.” A hymn from around 1250 describes “bondes ben leid on Symeon.”

 

Those physical restraints soon assumed another meaning: obligation. Around 1330, Robert Manning of Brunne’s “Story of England” referred to “ye bondes of homage.”

 

From there it was a short leap for the word to represent a pledge or a person’s word of honor. The modern phrase “my word is my bond” echoes a version of the Lancelot legend around 1500: “O kingis word shuld be a kingis bonde.”

 

By the late 16th century, the word had taken on a specific financial meaning. In Shakespeare’s “The Merchant of Venice,” Shylock agrees to lend Antonio 3,000 ducats for three months if Antonio will “go with me to a notary [and] seal me there your single bond.”

 

Shylock’s repayment, if Antonio defaulted, would be “an equal pound of your fair flesh.” Shakespeare probably chose that image deliberately. The word covenant, from the Latin convenire, “to come together,” had been used in English for nearly 300 years, often interchangeably with bond. In the book of Genesis, God sealed the covenant with Abraham by enjoining him to “circumscribe the flesh of your foreskin.” Shylock’s pound of flesh invokes this divine commandment, which would have been familiar to everyone in early modern Europe as governments began using bonds as financial instruments.

 

The word bond should remind everyone—borrowers and investors alike—that debt is meant to be a binding commitment. When the issuers of bonds no longer fear having to surrender a pound of flesh and they view their commitment as anything less than binding, bonds become little more than oral promises. And oral promises aren’t worth the paper they aren’t written on.

 

This is the latest in a series on the origin and history of financial words. You can read the earlier installments here:
* hedge fund
* fund
* credit
* volatile
* realize
* mania
* money
* stock
* cash
* inflation

 
 
Oscar Edward Cesare, “Bonds—Which?” (New York Evening Post, May 18, 1917). The choice here is between buying Liberty Bonds, which financed the U.S. military during World War I, and being shackled by “Prussia,” or Germany. Uncle Sam used to take the bondage thing a lot more seriously. LIBRARY OF CONGRESS
 
 
 

Money Mailbag

 

Have a question you’d like me to answer?

 

Want to weigh in on what you just read? Got a tip on something that I or my colleagues should investigate? Itching to tell me I’m wrong about something?

 

Just email intelligentinvestor@wsj.com. Don’t forget to include your name and location.

 

Q: Can you help me understand the difference between the 30-day SEC yield and the trailing 12-month distribution yield? Which is more important?
—Eric MacGillis, Ohio

 

A: “Yield statistics are often treated as if they’re interchangeable, but they’re really measuring different things,” says Joyce Huang, head of multi-sector fixed-income client portfolio management at Vanguard.

 

“For bond funds,” she says, “the 30-day SEC yield is generally the best comparison tool between funds, because it’s standardized.” The SEC yield is based on a Securities and Exchange Commission formula, which you can view in detail on p. 57 of this PDF from the SEC. The SEC yield quantifies the latest 30 days of a portfolio’s investment income net of expenses, annualized. For money-market funds, the equivalent measure is the 7-day SEC yield.

 

By contrast, says Huang, “Distribution yield is backward-looking. It annualizes the income actually paid out recently, typically using the last month’s distribution. This measure can be useful because it reflects actual cash investors have recently received, but it may not represent what the funds will earn going forward.”

 

That’s especially true, adds Huang, “in a rapidly changing rate environment such as right now,” when “distribution yield can lag the portfolio’s current earning power” as rates rise.

 

Here’s another important distinction. For many ETFs, distribution yield includes return of capital and income from trading options contracts, which can vary enormously from month to month—and can also eat away at your principal. Many such funds with high distribution yields in the short run end up producing low or negative total returns in the long run.

 

That’s why, as the late financial analyst Raymond DeVoe warned, “More money has been lost reaching for yield than at the point of a gun.”

 

Be well and invest well,

 

Jason

— Warren Buffett
